pr_title: Refactor LIFX discovery to make it faster and more reliable
pr_body:
Signed-off-by: Avi Miller <me@dje.li>

## Breaking change

This PR changes the network adapters used to discover LIFX devices.
Instead of enabling all adapters on which LIFX devices appear, this
PR switches to only using the adapter(s) enabled in Home Assistant.




## Proposed change

Currently there is a race condition that occurs when bulbs respond
multiple times to the discovery broadcast and the integration tries 
to register the same bulb that's already mid-registering. 

This PR adds an in-flight discovery throttle that only allows one 
direct connection per bulb at a time to avoid that race condition.

This is faster because there is a limit to how many packets a bulb 
can process per second. So, the fewer packets we send, the faster 
the bulb can process the ones it receives. 

It's more reliable because there are less packets on the network,
less broadcasts over wifi and thus less overall traffic. This allows
us to reduce the amount of message retries as well.

Finally, it eliminates the "does not generate unique ID" error that 
was caused by multiple discoveries trying to register the same entity
at the same time but out of order.

@bdraco I've officially asked the LIFX team to update the public protocol with the new switch messages: https://github.com/LIFX/public-protocol/issues/6 and I've been talking to folks at LIFX about this directly too. I also have an alternative integration that uses Photons instead of `aiolifx` that I've been working on for a while now, mostly as a learning exercise to get my head around mapping Home Assistant's opinions with Photon's opinions.
I'll check back on this tomorrow as I want to make sure Anders has a chance to look at it before hitting merge.

> Would that allow me to replace `aiolifx` with something else that may or may not be Photons?

Yeah. Well, it's almost the other way around: doing a big change like that requires you to sign up as code owner to make sure you are notified of the inevitable fallout.

As a code owner, it's somewhat expected that you track new issues. But you're a volunteer and nobody will hold it against you if you cannot donate enough time to resolve everything.

There is no actual rule but in practise being a code owner also means that you get priority in reviews since people will assume that a) you know what you are doing and b) you will be around to fix up any mistakes.

review_comments:
I wonder if the race could be fixed by just not adding the entity if it turns out that it was already added while we were getting the product info. Then we would not need the new dictionary.

```suggestion
                if bulb.mac_addr in self.entities:
                    _LOGGER.debug("Ignoring concurrently connected %s", entity.who)
                else:
                    _LOGGER.debug("Connected to %s", entity.who)
                    self.entities[bulb.mac_addr] = entity
                    self.async_add_entities([entity], True)
```

I thought about this but I wanted to stop the second or subsequent attempts before they even start to try and reduce overall network traffic. If we only check here, all that discovery is still being done. 

Let me take another look when I'm not on my phone and back at my desk tomorrow.
Yeah, this is too late in the process. The idea behind adding `discoveries_inflight` is tha I don't want Home Assistant to send any additional packets to the bulb.

This has nothing to do with discovery. It is the number of resends that we will do for unicast messages that expect a response but the response does not show up within `MESSAGE_TIMEOUT`.

I tested quite a lot before settling on the high value, some bulbs would stop responding for 5+ seconds (I tested with Gen2 back then).

If this is to reduce load on the bulbs you could consider increasing the timeout so the total duration stays the same but with fewer packets sent.

Again, I am not opposing this change, just telling you some history so you know what to look out for :)
My plan is to make these adjustable at the config entry level so folks can tweak the knobs to suit their own needs.
I actually prefer `1.0` to show that it can also be a fraction but that's just me.
This will be obvious when the knobs are user adjustable

Add `network` as a dep in `manifest.json`

`  "dependencies": ["network"],`
~I'm fairly sure I did.~ Yep, done. :)
Good call on cleaning up those texts 👍

The assumption was that aiolifx would handle this and only call us once: https://github.com/frawau/aiolifx/blob/b6ab48ad57457d3995d75f6149ffc5187e71f3a8/aiolifx/aiolifx.py#L195

But I guess that does not work. Maybe because of a register/unregister/register cycle and we do not cancel our `register_new_bulb` on `unregister`?

I have a few theories on this as I see the same thing happening with my Photons-powered integration. I _think_ it's because it relies on the zeroconf/HomeKit mDNS to trigger discovery instead of handling it internally, and it may be getting triggered multiple times.

My gut feeling is that this is the real issue and this PR is papering over it so it won't get properly fixed.

From your "home-assistant-current.log":
```
2022-04-25 09:45:52 DEBUG (MainThread) [homeassistant.components.lifx.light] 192.168.42.203 register NEW
[...]
2022-04-25 09:45:53 DEBUG (MainThread) [homeassistant.components.lifx.light] 192.168.42.203 register NEW
```

The above should never happen since discoveries are 1 minute apart. Also, the race in `register_new_bulb()` should not be an issue because aiolifx guards us.

All your bulbs register twice so I suspect that you are somehow running two discovery tasks. Unfortunately, I do not see that issue myself and the logging is very sparse so I am unable to figure out what happens :-(

(I can reproduce the "unique IDs" issue by setting an IP alias on my network interface so ifaddr finds two addresses with the same broadcast address)

Maybe this could help to uncover the underlying issue?

```diff
--- a/aiolifx/aiolifx.py
+++ b/aiolifx/aiolifx.py
@@ -1431,6 +1431,9 @@ class LifxScan:
             lifx_discovery = LifxDiscovery(self.loop, manager)
             discoveries.append(lifx_discovery)
             lifx_discovery.start(listen_ip=ip)
+            print(f"Starting discovery on {ip}")
+            import traceback
+            traceback.print_stack()
             tasks.append(self.loop.create_task(manager.lifx_ip()))

         (done, pending) = await aio.wait(tasks, timeout=timeout)
```

Yes, I am running multiple discovery tasks because I have both a wired and wifi connection on my development machine. I suspect this happens a lot though, as many Raspberry Pis would be configured the same way.

In my Photons-based integration, I determine the preferred interface for each broadcast network, but `aiolifx` doesn't do this. It just happily starts multiple scans. By limiting the discoveries in-flight, this eliminates the race condition that occurs on misconfigured multi-homed devices.

I don't see this as papering over the real issue, though. I can't change how people chose to configure their systems (and it seems I have to take another look at how macOS is configured wrt networking), but this refactor at least nullifies its impact.

The setup process with two discoveries is:
```
  wired: discovery request -> 60x discovery response -> feature request -> feature response -> [add entity]
  wifi: discovery request -> 60x discovery response -> feature request -> feature response -> [duplicate ID]
```

This PR proposes to ignore the second discovery response. That saves the unicast feature request for the duplicate entry (and thus avoids the duplicate ID warning):
```
  wired: discovery request -> 60x discovery response -> feature request -> feature response -> [add entity]
  wifi: discovery request -> 60x discovery response -> [ignore]
```

However, what we really want is just a single discovery since that will furthermore save a redundant broadcast and all the matching responses from each bulb:
```
  wired: discovery request -> 60x discovery response -> feature request -> feature response -> [add entity]
  wifi: [idle]
```

So I think the bug is with the network detection (i.e. the ifaddr usage in aiolifx), not really `register_new_bulb()`.

Fair enough. I think I can leverage HA's own networking helpers to limit discovery to whichever interface has been selected for mDNS by HA, and then limit aiolifx to that network interface. 

It's what I'm doing for my Photons integration anyway, I just need to modify it for aiolifx.
Awesome. You might find that adjusting the retries does not matter then because bulbs do not get overloaded in the first place.

@amelchio four years ago, you added this line:
```
lifx_ip_addresses = await aiolifx().LifxScan(hass.loop).scan()
```

Any objection if I just remove this line and instead, only enable LIFX discovery on network interfaces enabled by Home Assistant?

That sounds reasonable. HA did not have any interface selector back then :)

It's a breaking change, of course – but not in a bad way.

How much do we want to protect users from themselves? Specifically: if someone choses to manually enable multiple interfaces on the same broadcast network, the current behaviour will re-occur, unless we specifically check for that as well. 

I'm actually happy with this option because I'd document the badness that would occur if such a configuration is chosen by the user and it would mean we could just let Home Assistant's network config be authorative. 

Thoughts?

Alternatively, I keep this fix in place as well, which means if someone _does_ enable multiple interfaces that trigger duplicate discovery, we at least ignore some of it at the cost of additional network traffic.

(Perhaps with a log entry stating "multiple broadcast discoveries detectied, ignoring...")

For that situation I would propose my one-line fix from yesterday but upgraded to a warning since we now realized that it is a situation to avoid: https://github.com/home-assistant/core/pull/70458#discussion_r857101697

I personally think that's a fine balance between usability and code complexity. However, @bdraco can probably comment on how other integrations handle this (i.e. being enabled for wired/wifi interfaces on the same subnet)
Except that still sends the unicast responses on the second interface, which we want to avoid.
I would personally not complicate the code with the in-flight dictionary just to cater for misconfigurations – but I think that is the kind of judgement call that a code owner should be making :-)
I see what you did there. :)

Checking the configured network interfaces is a nice improvement 👍 

You'll definitely find that you'll still have the same issue since there are still all kinds of "strange" network setups.  We end up with lots of code in zeroconf to handle these type of problems with overlapping responses since even with the ability to configure it, its still quite a common issue.

As much as it would be nice to to have these type of issues, I think you are stuck with either tracking the discoveries to avoid dupes as you have now, or some type of locking (usually less preferred).   I've tried to remove similar code in zeroconf and always end up having to put it back.

Here is a section from RFC6762 that highlights how different implementations can be https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6762.html#section-6.2
```
   Some Multicast DNS responders treat a physical interface with both
   IPv4 and IPv6 address as a single interface with two addresses.
   Other Multicast DNS responders may treat this case as logically two
   interfaces (one with one or more IPv4 addresses, and the other with
   one or more IPv6 addresses), but responders that operate this way
   MUST NOT put the corresponding automatic NSEC records in replies they
   send (i.e., a negative IPv4 assertion in their IPv6 responses, and a
   negative IPv6 assertion in their IPv4 responses) because this would
   cause incorrect operation in responders on the network that work the
   former way.
```
Yeah, it makes quite the difference for performance and stability, too. I'm happy keeping the in-flight check as a backup for those network configs that are on the more insane side.

@bdraco Can you clarify a bit ... I understand your experience that a request can have multiple responses but is the change here (i.e. to use the configured network interfaces) sufficient to keep _us_ from sending multiple requests in the first place?

@amelchio no, it's not, because HA still allows a user to manually enable multiple interfaces on the same logical network, which would result in multiple broadcasts to the same IP broadcast network. However, the likelihood of this configuration is pretty low.

I am not asking whether people will shoot their feet but rather if they are able to avoid it.

(Like I said, I'm down with you change; just trying to fully understand the situation)
Gotcha. It's certainly avoidable: just leave the network config on Auto, or ensure that if you do have multiple interfaces enabled, they're on different IP networks.

It is avoidable except when they actually need to broadcast on multiple interfaces because they have multiple subnets.  We have users that have their IoT subnet, their secure subnet, etc so we should expect they are going to turn on multiple interfaces and we may get broadcast traffic from one reflected back on another.

Multiple distinct subnets should be fine as LIFX uses UDP broadcast for discovery, which is rarely reflected, repeated or routed.

Multiple enabled interfaces on the same subnet however, will generate duplicate responses.

This is usually what happens when someone enables both wifi and a wired connection on an RPi, for example.

> Multiple distinct subnets should be fine as LIFX uses UDP broadcast for discovery, which is rarely reflected, repeated or routed.

Take a look at the python-zeroconf issue queue history, it may paint a slightly different view on how you define rarely (in fairness issues only see the problems)

> 
> Multiple enabled interfaces on the same subnet however, will generate duplicate responses.

Yes

> 
> This is usually what happens when someone enables both wifi and a wired connection on an RPi, for example.

If you have wired I would considering enabling wifi as well a bad idea but it happens all the time unfortunately.
In a future PR we should return above, drop the else, and outdent below
I _think_ I get what you're suggesting. Will try it out and see what happens.

I'm not entirely sure what the point of this block is any more. Instead of just this minor change, I'd prefer to refactor the whole discovery process as a whole, while moving it out of the light entity as well.
I can explain but I am not sure which block you are talking about. Will look at the logs now.

@amelchio I've mostly worked it out and it's still somewhat relevant given the current discovery process. I got a single `missing entity_id` error when I first tested @bdraco's suggestion, but I can't seem to repeat that. I'd like to get this merged and tested in the beta though, and will continue to optimise where I can.
I have had some debugging sessions where the IP address was useful; in particular, I remember it being the router address in some situations.

I really want to switch to using the LIFX serial instead of the MAC address, because that matches the official app. 

When that happens, I'll bring the IP address back, most likely.
